verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, a psalm, of David, a song.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster: a psalm of David, a song.
verses.directors_commentary: This is a title, not part of the song, and the Hebrew counts it as verse 1, which is why the KJV's numbers run one behind through the whole psalm (KJV 65:1 is the Hebrew verse 2). The KJV's 'chief Musician' is a guess at לַמְנַצֵּחַ, from the root נצח, 'to be preeminent, to oversee'; it names an overseer of the temple music, or perhaps the one who leads the performance. 'A psalm' and 'a song' are two genre words set side by side: the first suggests a piece sung to an instrument, the second a piece sung. Radak and Meiri read the psalm as one for the exile; Malbim ties it to rain after famine, and the verses that follow lean toward Malbim. Tell your singers to treat this as an announcement: the leader names the piece, the people settle.

philological_notes.note: Participle with lamed: 'for the one who oversees/excels'. The title appears in 55 psalm headings. The sense 'choirmaster' fits the temple setting; the KJV's 'chief Musician' is the same idea.
sources: Targum on Psalms 65:1 renders it 'to praise'

verses.translation_literal: To you, silence [is] praise, God, in Zion, and to you a vow will be paid.
verses.translation_dramatic: Before you, O God, in Zion, even silence is praise. The voice falls still, and the stillness is the song. And to you the vow will be paid in full.
verses.directors_commentary: The first half is among the strangest openings in the Psalter, and every English version smooths it. דֻמִיָּה is not 'waiteth': it is the noun 'silence', and the verse literally says 'to you silence is praise'. Rashi hears an overwhelmed worshipper: praise has no end, and whoever piles on epithets only subtracts, so silence is the honest hymn. Metzudat David says the same, that to limit God with titles is to shrink him. Radak and Meiri take the word instead as 'waiting' (as in 'stand still' in 1 Samuel 14:9): praise waits in readiness. That second reading is why the KJV, ASV and Webster say 'waiteth for thee'; the BBE ('it is right for you') drops the word altogether. Play it as a held breath in the courtyard. The second half is the commercial and ritual reality: a נֶדֶר was a conditional promise made in distress ('if you rescue me, I will bring a sacrifice'), and 'will be paid' means the pilgrims who prayed in the drought now come up to Zion with their animals and flour. Malbim adds a sharp touch: for this God the vow is not conditional, because rescue is certain. The KJV's 'Sion' is a Greek-Latin spelling of Zion, the temple mount at Jerusalem.

philological_notes.note: Noun 'silence, stillness' (cf. Ps 62:2 דּוּמִיָּה, 'my soul is silent'). The tradition splits between 'silence is praise' (Rashi, Metzudat David, Malbim) and 'praise waits' (Radak, Meiri, Ibn Ezra).
A vow: a promise made in a crisis, to be paid once the help came. 'Will be paid' (יְשֻׁלַּם) uses the root שׁלם, 'to make whole'; paying a vow completes it.

verses.translation_literal: Hearer of prayer, to you all flesh will come.
verses.translation_dramatic: O you who hear prayer, to you all flesh will come, every living creature that breathes and needs.
verses.directors_commentary: 'Hearer of prayer' is a title spoken straight to God, a direct address without a verb; the KJV's 'O thou that hearest' is fine, though it turns a title into a clause. The weight is on 'all flesh', כָּל־בָּשָׂר, the same phrase that elsewhere describes all living beings, human and animal, in their weakness. It is not 'all people who are godly'; the psalm says every frail creature is on the road to this one door. Radak gives a charming reason in the voice of a royal courtier: a human king can hear two or three petitioners, never everyone, but this God hears everyone at once, each with his own prayer. Malbim makes the same point from the palace: the common petitioner has to go through the king's officers, but here no one stands between. Actors should know this is the hinge of the psalm: the particular worshipper at Zion becomes the whole world arriving. The KJV, in 'shall all flesh come', makes it a prediction; the Hebrew imperfect can equally mean 'keep coming', a habit.

philological_notes.note: 'All flesh': every living creature, stressing mortal weakness. The scope is wider than Israel; the context favours people of every nation (cf. 'all the ends of the earth' in verse 6).
Poetic form of 'to you', the preposition עַד with a pronominal ending, the same form as in Job 4:5.

verses.translation_literal: Words of iniquities are too strong for me; our transgressions, you, you atone for them.
verses.translation_dramatic: The weight of my guilt is too heavy for me. It has grown stronger than I am. But our wrongs, our rebellions: you, you cover them over.
verses.directors_commentary: Listen to the pronouns. A single voice says 'than me', then the whole congregation says 'our'; Radak and Meiri hear the people speaking as one person, and Rashi hears them admitting they cannot list every sin and so ask for forgiveness in a single clause. The KJV's 'Iniquities prevail against me' is close, but it loses the opening דִּבְרֵי, 'words/matters of', which is a Hebrew way to say 'things', and it loses the stress on 'you', which is spoken twice in effect: אַתָּה, 'you', stands first in its clause, an emphatic pronoun. Malbim hears something daring: the sins are stronger than man, and they themselves become advocates, arguing that only God can undo what humans cannot resist. The KJV's 'purge them away' tries to render תְּכַפְּרֵם. The root כפר is the sacrificial vocabulary of the temple: to cover, to wipe clean, to atone, as the high priest does on the Day of Atonement. The ASV's 'forgive' is looser. The scene turns: from a pilgrim at the gate who has just promised a vow, to the confession that makes entering the courts possible.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'words/matters of iniquities'. Meaning 'things of guilt'; Malbim reads the iniquities as speaking in the sinner's defence.
'Were stronger than me' (comparative min): the sins got the upper hand, as in the same verb for floodwaters that 'prevailed' (Gen 7).
Piel of כפר: the technical verb for cultic atonement ('cover over, wipe away'). The verb is God's own act here, not the priest's.

verses.translation_literal: Happy [is the one] you choose and bring near; he dwells [in] your courts. May we be satisfied with the goodness of your house, the holy [place] of your temple.
verses.translation_dramatic: Happy the one you choose, the one you draw close, who may live within your courts. Let us be filled, let us eat our fill, with the goodness of your house, the holy of holies of your temple.
verses.directors_commentary: אַשְׁרֵי is the cry of someone looking at a person whose road is straight: 'how blessed!', and it is plural-construct in form, as if saying 'the happinesses of'. KJV 'Blessed is the man' adds 'man' and joins the relative without a marker; Ibn Ezra notes the Hebrew leaves out 'whom'. The choice is God's, not the man's: תִּבְחַר, 'you choose', and וּתְקָרֵב, 'you bring near', the vocabulary of sacrifice and priesthood (the verb קרב is the one used of bringing an offering near). To 'dwell in the courts' is the dream of a temple servant or a pilgrim who never leaves. The courtyard, the house and the temple form three rings, as Meiri shows, each deeper than the last: חצר, בית, היכל. Then the meal: נִשְׂבְּעָה means 'we are filled, sated' like those who eat at a sacrificial feast, so the KJV's 'we shall be satisfied' is tame. And the last phrase, קְדֹשׁ הֵיכָלֶךָ, is an adjective in the construct: literally 'the holy of your temple', whose most holy part is the inner chamber (Meiri: הדביר). The KJV's 'even of thy holy temple' smooths it.

philological_notes.note: An exclamation of congratulation ('oh the happiness of'), distinct from the blessing בָּרוּךְ; the KJV's 'blessed' blurs the two.
Piel 'you bring near', the verb of approaching God or the altar; the choice and the nearness are God's act.
First-person plural, spoken as a wish or a statement: 'let us be sated'. The congregation, not the single chosen man, speaks.

verses.translation_literal: [With] awesome [deeds] in righteousness you answer us, God of our salvation, the trust of all the ends of the earth and [of the] distant sea.
verses.translation_dramatic: With deeds that make the heart stand still, with justice, you answer us, God of our rescue: the one in whom the whole earth puts its trust, to its farthest edge, and the far-off sea beyond.
verses.directors_commentary: The word נוֹרָאוֹת is 'things that inspire awe or dread' (from ירא, 'to fear'), and the KJV's 'terrible things' is a victim of language change: in 1611 'terrible' still meant 'awe-inspiring'; today it means 'bad'. Say 'awesome' without the slang. In the world of the psalm the answer to prayer comes as a sign of power, in rain and in the overthrow of enemies, and it comes 'in righteousness', that is, in keeping with justice, not whim (Rashi: God does awesome acts against the nations). The second half widens the circle: God is the מִבְטָח, the safe place for trust, for people at קַצְוֵי־אֶרֶץ, 'the ends of the earth', and for the 'distant sea'. The word 'ends' stands for both the earth and the sea (Radak, Meiri: it applies to each noun), and 'distant' is plural, so the sea-peoples are far from the temple in every direction. The KJV's relative 'who art the confidence of all the ends of the earth, and of them that are afar off upon the sea' turns a place into people and adds 'upon'. Keep it bare. The pun: 'answer us' (תַּעֲנֵנוּ, from ענה) belongs to a root that can also mean 'to afflict'; here God answers with action.

philological_notes.note: Niphal participle of 'to fear': 'fear-inspiring things', neither 'terrible' in the modern sense nor merely 'wonderful'. The same word is used for the great acts of the Exodus.
'Place or object of trust, refuge'. The psalmist makes the God of Zion the trust of the whole inhabited world.
'Ends of the earth', the remotest regions, with 'sea' balancing it; the preceding construct serves both nouns.

verses.translation_literal: Establishing mountains by his strength, being girded with might.
verses.translation_dramatic: He sets the mountains in their places, and they stand by his strength alone, and he wears might about him as a man wears his belt.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm turns here from the temple and its answered prayer to the whole creation, and the actors should feel the scale change: from a courtyard to the horizon. The verse is built from two participles with no finite verb, so it reads like a title being pronounced over the next lines. The participle מֵכִין, 'establishing', comes from כון, the root of firm founding and making ready. The psalm returns to that root twice in verse 10, in תָּכִין and תְּכִינֶהָ: the God who set the mountains in place is the one who 'prepares' the grain and the earth. Rashi hears the same link, quoting Psalm 147:8, 'who prepares rain for the earth, who makes the mountains sprout'.

The KJV's 'setteth fast the mountains' is sound, but its 'being girded with power' hides a picture. אָזַר is to tie on a belt, and in the ancient world a man gathered his long robe into a belt before work or a fight. So God puts on strength as a workman or warrior does (Radak: might is his belt, and he never borrows it). BBE's 'robed with power' loses the belt altogether. Mountains were also the places where the gods of Canaan were thought to live, so this line claims them for YHWH as his own handiwork.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil participle of כון, 'to establish, to make firm, to prepare'. The verb returns twice in verse 10 (תָּכִין, תְּכִינֶהָ), so the God who sets up mountains also sets up the harvest.
Niphal participle of אָזַר, 'to gird'. It is the image of tying on the belt before action; God wears might as a belt.

verses.translation_literal: Who calms the roar of the seas, the roar of their waves, and the tumult of the peoples.
verses.translation_dramatic: He quiets the roar of the seas, the roar of their breaking waves, and he quiets the tumult of the nations.
verses.directors_commentary: Repeat the word. שְׁאוֹן, 'roar, crash', is said twice, 'the roar of the seas, the roar of their waves', so the second echo makes the sound louder before it is stilled; the KJV keeps the repetition ('noise ... noise'), though its 'noise' is flat for a word of crashing surf, and the BBE drops it. A reader hears the surf pounding, and then the third item comes without warning: וַהֲמוֹן לְאֻמִּים, 'the din of the peoples'. The sea and the nations are a single image; for the ancient Near East the sea was chaos, and the crowd of foreign nations was chaos too. God does the same thing to both. Here is the polemic: in Canaanite myth Baal had to fight Yam, the sea god, to impose order; here the sea is not a rival but a noise God turns down. מַשְׁבִּיחַ is rare: it means 'to still, to soothe' (Rashi relates it to 'bring low'; compare Psalm 89:10, 'you still them'). The KJV's 'the people' flattens לְאֻמִּים, which is plural, 'peoples, nations'.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil participle meaning 'to calm, quiet, subdue'. The same consonants שבח also give the common verb 'to praise' in later Hebrew; here the sense is 'calm', as in Ps 89:10.
'Crash, roar' of waves and of armies; here repeated for effect and then paired with the human 'tumult'.

verses.translation_literal: And the dwellers of the ends are afraid of your signs; the goings-out of morning and evening you make shout for joy.
verses.translation_dramatic: And those who live at the edges of the world are struck with awe at your signs. The places where morning comes out and where evening goes in: you set them singing.
verses.directors_commentary: The KJV's 'are afraid at thy tokens' has two problems. 'Tokens' is archaic for אֹתוֹת, 'signs, portents', things like thunder, lightning and rain-bearing clouds (Metzudat David) or the sun, moon and stars (Radak, Meiri). And 'uttermost parts' loses the repetition from verse 6: it is the same 'ends' (קְצָוֹת), now the people who live there. The verb is 'they fear' with a vav-consecutive form, in the past tense; Meiri and Radak read it as a prophecy. The second half is the poetry. מוֹצָאֵי בֹקֶר וָעֶרֶב, 'the exits of morning and evening', the places where the day comes out and goes in: east and west, sunrise and sunset. The verb תַּרְנִין is a causative of 'to shout for joy': the KJV's 'to rejoice' is weaker; God makes the horizons ring. Rashi hears the blessings of the day in this: every morning the nations say the blessing for the lights, every evening the blessing for the dusk. Direct the actors so that the fear and the joy come in the same breath, as in the awe of a thunderstorm after a dry season.

philological_notes.note: 'Signs': visible marks of divine action, here the weather and the heavenly bodies. Not 'tokens' in the modern sense.
'Goings-out of morning': the east where the day emerges; paired with evening, the west. Read by Radak and Meiri as the sun, moon and stars.
Hiphil 'you cause to ring out with joy', a loud shout rather than a quiet gladness.

verses.translation_literal: You have visited the earth and you made it overflow; much you make it rich; the stream of God is full of water; you prepare their grain, for thus you prepare it.
verses.translation_dramatic: You came to the earth, and found her parched, and you made her overflow. You have enriched her past counting. The river of God is brimming with water, and from it you make ready their grain. This is how you ready the land.
verses.directors_commentary:
The earth is the subject of a visit, and the actors should play it as a visit: the Hebrew verb פָּקַד is what a lord does when he calls on his property, or God when he remembers someone and acts. After the drought, it is the first sign of rain. The next verb, וַתְּשֹׁקְקֶהָ, is rare and its sense is debated. Rashi and Radak take it as 'you gave it drink' or 'you made it overflow'. Meiri and Radak also hear a link with שׁוּק, 'longing', so that God visits an earth that is already thirsty. The KJV's 'waterest' keeps the first sense and loses the second.

The verse ends on a deliberate echo. The root כון, 'to prepare, make firm', appears twice, in תָּכִין and תְּכִינֶהָ, and it picks up מֵכִין from verse 7: God who established the mountains now prepares the grain, so the same hand makes ready the soil, the rain and the crop. The KJV, with 'preparest' and 'provided', cannot show that it is one verb. 'The river of God', for פֶּלֶג אֱלֹהִים, makes the actors ask what the stream is. Rashi and the Targum say it is a heavenly reservoir, full of rain. Radak has a different picture: when the earth has drunk, large streams are left over on the ground, and 'of God' only means 'great'. Palestine's farmers had no great rivers and depended on winter rain, so for them the rain itself was the river that never failed.

philological_notes.note: 'Stream of God'. Rashi and the Targum read it as a heavenly reservoir, the Targum's 'storehouse of God which is in heaven', full of rain, from which the grain is prepared. Radak reads it differently: streams are left on the ground after the earth has drunk its fill, and 'of God' marks them as great, as in 'a great city of God'. Metzudat David and Metzudat Zion take פֶּלֶג as a water channel.
Hiphil of כון, 'to prepare'. It occurs twice in this verse (תָּכִין, תְּכִינֶהָ) and echoes מֵכִין in verse 7.

Of uncertain sense. Ibn Ezra rejects the view that it means 'you made it drink' (ותשקיה), and Radak and Meiri connect it with longing (שׁוּק, תְּשׁוּקָה), so that God visits an earth that already longed for rain.

verses.translation_literal: Its furrows, drenching; settling its ridges; with showers you soften it; its sprouting you bless.
verses.translation_dramatic: Its furrows, drink until they are full. Its ridges, you press them down and settle them. With soft showers you melt the clods, and what sprouts from the soil, you bless.
verses.directors_commentary: This is a plowman's verse, and the Hebrew keeps it terse: there are almost no connectors. The KJV and ASV swap 'ridges' and 'furrows' for the same two nouns, which shows how uncertain they are. תְּלָמִים are the ploughed rows (Rashi: the lines of the plough); גְּדוּדִים are the ridges between or the cut sides. Radak places the 'furrows' as the soil heaps and 'ridges' as the depressions; the sense is that every row is soaked and every crest is settled. 'You press down' (נַחֵת) is the beating rain that flattens the loose earth; some read it as 'level', some as 'bring down'. תְּמֹגְגֶנָּה, 'you melt it', means to soften and dissolve, like a hardened clod turned to dough; the KJV's 'makest it soft' is good. רְבִיבִים are gentle spring showers (Metzudat Zion cites Deut 32:2, 'like showers on the grass'), not storms: fine, soaking drops that soften the ground without washing it away. Then the blessing: 'its sprouting you bless', God blesses the first green tips, the moment a farmer in a drought year had feared would never come.

philological_notes.note: 'Showers, light rain', as in Deut 32:2. The tone is gentle and abundant, not a flood.
Polel of מוג 'to melt, dissolve': hard soil is made soft. The KJV 'makest it soft' is fair.
The ploughed rows ('furrows'); English versions swap this with גְּדוּדֶיהָ 'ridges'.

verses.translation_literal: You have crowned the year of your goodness, and your tracks drip fatness.
verses.translation_dramatic: You have crowned the year with your goodness as with a wreath, and where your wheels have passed, richness falls in drops.
verses.directors_commentary:
The year is a king or a bride, and the verb עִטַּרְתָּ gives it a crown (עֲטָרָה). Ibn Ezra's image is a queen among the maidens. Here 'goodness' is the harvest year itself. The KJV's 'with thy goodness' turns 'the year of your goodness' into a year crowned by something, but the Hebrew makes the goodness the year's possession. Say the line as a coronation.

The second half has a picture the KJV smooths. מַעְגָּלֶיךָ are 'your tracks', the ruts or circles that a cart or chariot leaves. Metzudat Zion and Radak identify them with the clouds, which are God's road across the sky (Job 22:14, 'the vault of heaven he walks'). So the clouds are the tracks of a God who drives over the land, and they drip. Rashi reads them as the heavens. 'Fatness', דֶּשֶׁן, is not oil. Rashi, Metzudat Zion and Meiri gloss it שׁוּמָן, 'fat, richness': the rain is rich because it fattens the soil, the crop and the flocks. The KJV's 'paths' makes it a road, and the Hebrew cart-track is more physical.

philological_notes.note: 'Your tracks', the ruts or circular course of a wheel. Metzudat Zion and Radak identify them with the clouds, God's route over the sky. Rashi reads them as the heavens.
'Fatness', richness. Rashi and Metzudat Zion both gloss it שׁוּמָן, 'fat, richness'.

verses.translation_literal: They drip [on] the pastures of [the] wilderness, and [with] rejoicing hills they gird themselves.
verses.translation_dramatic: They drip on the wilderness pastures, on the land where the shepherds lead, and the hills tie joy about their waists like a belt.
verses.directors_commentary:
The subject has not changed. 'Your tracks', the clouds of the last verse, are still dripping, and they now do so onto the pastures of the wilderness. The Hebrew has no 'upon': Rashi supplies 'the heavens drip on the pastures of the wilderness', and Meiri says outright that the word על is missing. The KJV adds 'upon' and moves on. A reading in which the pastures themselves drip exists, but it is grammatically strained: the verb יִרְעֲפוּ is masculine plural and נְאוֹת is feminine plural, so the verb agrees with 'tracks' (מַעְגָּלֶיךָ) and not with the pastures. Play it as the rain reaching beyond the farmland.

The wilderness here is מִדְבָּר, not a desert of sand but the dry grazing country where shepherds take their flocks (Ibn Ezra: 'the dwellings of shepherds'). The rain falls where no one plants, and Radak says the animals find food and drink there. The second half repeats the belt of verse 7, which is a quiet frame: God girds himself with might, the hills gird themselves with joy (תַּחְגֹּרְנָה, from חָגַר). The KJV's 'rejoice on every side' drops the garment. Radak notes the hills had put on sackcloth in the drought and now put on joy in its place.

philological_notes.note: 'Pastures', 'dwellings' of shepherds. Ibn Ezra compares נוֹת רוֹעִים and Metzudat Zion glosses it as a dwelling place.
'They gird themselves', the belt image of verse 7 (נֶאְזָר) in another verb. Radak contrasts the sackcloth the hills wore in the drought with the joy they now wear.

verses.translation_literal: The pastures have put on the flock [or: the rams among the flock are clothed (with fat), Metzudat David]; and valleys wrap themselves [in] grain; they shout for joy, indeed they sing.
verses.translation_dramatic: The meadows put on the flocks as a garment, and the valleys wrap themselves in grain. They shout for joy. They sing.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends on clothing, and the actors should hear the wardrobe: the verbs לָבְשׁוּ, 'they put on', and יַעַטְפוּ, 'they wrap themselves', follow the girded hills of verse 13. The land has been naked in the drought and is now dressed, with flocks on the pastures and grain in the valleys.

The difficulty is כָרִים. It can mean 'pastures, meadows' (Ibn Ezra: a wide כַּר, as the parallel 'valleys' shows; Radak: level ground), or rams and lambs (Metzudat Zion: lambs), and the sense changes the picture. Rashi and Radak keep the pastures: the pastures put on the flock, which lies across the plain like wool and hides the ground. Metzudat David reads the animals: the rams among the flock are clothed in flesh and fat. The KJV's 'clothed with flocks' follows the first reading and softens the verb to a passive. The verbs of the last line, 'shout for joy' (יִתְרוֹעֲעוּ) and 'sing', are plural: the subject is the valleys and everything in them. Radak says the heavy ears of grain make a sound in the wind as if they sang. The psalm ends in noise after the silence of drought.

philological_notes.note: 'Pastures, meadows' (a broad כַּר) or 'rams, lambs'. Rashi, Radak and Ibn Ezra take it as pastures; Metzudat David and Metzudat Zion take it as sheep. STEPBible has 'pastures'.
'Grain'. Metzudat Zion compares לִשְׁבֹּר בָּר מִמִּצְרָיִם, 'to buy grain from Egypt' (Genesis 42).
